1366.title: Sh-B-T
1366.hook: Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease
1366.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat stop work from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and the rabbis' detailed categories of work, set out in the Mishnah and Talmud, guide what is set down for the day; practice varies across communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Z-K-R: zachor and zikaron, memory that does something. Your line was memory is doing. A new week starts today, with three letters that stop.

One morning in the book of Joshua, the people walk out of their tents and there's nothing on the ground. Through the wilderness journey, bread had come down from the sky and lay on the ground in the mornings. Now they've crossed into the land and eaten its grain, and the text says it plainly: "And the manna ceased on the morrow." No miracle announced. No speech. It just stopped. The verb for ceased is built from the same three letters as a word you already know, the name of a whole day of the week.
screen: `NO MANNA ON THE GROUND.` → `THE MANNA CEASED.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Sh-B-T. Shin, bet, tav. Shabbat. You met it on day eleven as the oldest labor law; today, the root under it. First, creation. Genesis says God finished the work, "and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." Rested, in the English. In Hebrew, the verb is from this root: stopped, ceased. The text doesn't say God was tired. It says the making stopped. Second, the opposite promise. After the flood, God tells Noah that "day and night shall not cease." The same root again. The world's rhythms never stop, and inside them, once a week, people do. Third, who stops. The commandment in Exodus lists the son and the daughter, the servants, the animals, and "thy stranger that is within thy gates." Shabbat isn't a rest for those who can afford it. Everyone in the household stops together. Fourth, stopping is a skill. The rabbis of the Mishnah gave whole chapters to defining what counts as work on Shabbat, so stopping could be clear and shared, not a vague good intention. Notice the name. The day isn't called after its meals, prayers or songs. It's called after what people stop. Ceasing comes first, and the rest grows in the space it leaves.
screen: `THE MAKING STOPPED.` · `DAY AND NIGHT SHALL NOT CEASE.` · `EVERYONE IN THE HOUSE STOPS.` · `STOPPING IS A SKILL.` · then, large: `TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Put down whatever is in your hands, leave any open screen alone, and notice the urge to do the next thing without doing it. Each time your mind starts making a list, let the list stop, the way the manna stopped: no speech, no fuss, just ceasing. If you pray, you can hold the word Shabbat on the breath, in and out.
Sh-B-T. Shin, bet, tav: to stop, to cease. The root of Shabbat, and of the manna that ceased. Today's word.
Your line: to stop. The world keeps its rhythm, and once a week people step out of it. See you on the next root.

1367.title: Sh-U-V
1367.hook: teshuvah, from the root to turn or return
1367.howItsDone: Teshuvah is a theme of the season from the month of Elul through Yom Kippur, and a blessing asking for return is also part of the weekday Amidah prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-B-T: the root of Shabbat, and of the manna that ceased. Your line was to stop. Today, a root for turning around.

Three widows stand on a road leading out of Moab. Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she tells her two daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' houses. "Turn again, my daughters," she says. Orpah kisses her and turns back. Ruth won't; she goes on with Naomi. Then the chapter ends with a strange line: Naomi returned, and Ruth with her, "which returned out of the country of Moab." Ruth returned. To a place she had never been. The verb doing all that turning and returning is today's root.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH TURNS BACK.` → `RUTH RETURNS, SOMEWHERE NEW.`

segments.voice: Sh-U-V. Shin, vav, vet. To turn, to return. From it comes teshuvah, the word often translated repentance; way back on day nineteen, you met it as return. Turn it four ways. First, Ruth. Her first chapter keeps coming back to this verb, and it lets Ruth return to a land she's never seen. So teshuvah isn't only going back to where you were. It can be turning toward where you belong. Second, the prophet's call. Hosea says: "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God." That verse is read on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and that Sabbath takes its name from it: Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath of Return. Third, both directions. Lamentations ends with a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Turn us, and we'll turn: asked for and done at the same time. Those words are sung in synagogue as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark. Fourth, how you know it's real. Maimonides, in his Laws of Teshuvah, says complete teshuvah is when the same situation comes around again, with the same pull, and the person, able to do the same thing, chooses differently. Not because the door is locked. Because they've turned. Not a feeling of regret, but a change of direction you can see.
screen: `RUTH RETURNS TO A NEW PLACE.` · `SHABBAT SHUVAH.` · `TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.` · `THE SAME CHOICE, CHOSEN DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TURN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you've drifted from: a call you keep not making, a habit that slipped, a person you've been short with. Don't build a case against yourself; just find the direction you've been facing and the one you'd rather face, and in your mind, make the turn. If you pray, you can say the words from Lamentations: turn us, and we shall be turned.
Sh-U-V. Shin, vav, vet: to turn, to return. The root of teshuvah, the turning a person can choose. Today's word.
Your line: turn. Teshuvah is a direction you can see, not only a feeling. Rest well.

1368.title: P-L-L
1368.hook: tefillah; the verb for praying is reflexive, and many read it as judging oneself
1368.howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah, the standing prayer of the daily services, quietly, with the lips moving and the voice low, a practice the Talmud draws from Hannah's prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-U-V: teshuvah, turning and returning. Your line was turn. Today, the root of the Hebrew word for prayer.

A woman is standing in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Her name is Hannah, and she has no children. Her lips are moving, but there's no sound. The book of Samuel says: "only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard." The priest Eli watches her, decides she's drunk, and tells her to put away her wine. She isn't drunk. She's pouring out her heart. The text says she "prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." Silent, inward, completely honest. What she was doing has a Hebrew word, and its three letters are today's root.
screen: `HANNAH AT SHILOH.` → `LIPS MOVING, NO VOICE.` → `ELI THINKS SHE'S DRUNK.`

segments.voice: P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed. From it comes tefillah, prayer. Turn it four ways. First, the courtroom. In Exodus, a fine is set, and a man "shall pay as the judges determine." Judges there is from this root: judging, weighing, deciding. Second, one verse that holds both. Eli warns his sons: "If one man sin against another, the judge shall judge him: but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him?" Judge, and intreat, which means plead or pray: the same letters, a few words apart. Third, the verb. To pray is l'hitpallel, built in a form Hebrew often uses for actions turned back on oneself, like getting dressed or washing up. Some teachers read it this way: to pray is to judge yourself, to stand in front of the truth about your own life. Others hear it as standing before the Judge, or as pleading. These readings sit side by side, and they don't cancel each other out. Fourth, Hannah. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, draws lessons about prayer from her: say the words in the heart, let the lips move, keep the voice low. Her prayer wasn't a performance for Eli or anyone. It was a long, honest look inward, said to God. So the root gives prayer a mirror as well as a window.
screen: `AS THE JUDGES DETERMINE.` · `JUDGE AND INTREAT, ONE VERSE.` · `A VERB TURNED BACK ON ONESELF.` · `HANNAH'S SILENT PRAYER.` · then, large: `PRAYER LOOKS INWARD.`

segments.voice: Let your face go still and ask one plain question about the last day: where was I at my best, and where did I fall short? Don't argue with the answer or dress it up; look the way a fair judge looks, clearly and without cruelty. If you pray, you can bring what you saw into your prayer, lips moving and voice low, the way Hannah did; if you don't, simply stay with what's true for a few breaths.
P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed: to judge, to plead, and in its turned-back form, to pray. The root of tefillah. Today's word.
Your line: prayer looks inward. A mirror first, then a window. I'll be here tomorrow.

1369.title: A-H-V
1369.howItsDone: The paragraph beginning 'and thou shalt love the LORD thy God' is said right after the first line of the Shema, morning and evening, and the blessing just before the Shema speaks of God's love for Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, P-L-L: tefillah, and the verb that turns back on itself. Your line was prayer looks inward. Today, the root of love.

Seven years is a long time to work for anyone. Jacob agrees to it, working for his uncle Laban, so that he can marry Laban's daughter Rachel. Seven years of flocks, heat and cold nights. And the Torah sums it all up in one sentence: "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Years that felt like days. That's what love did to the clock. The word for love in that verse is today's root.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS FOR RACHEL.` → `THEY SEEMED BUT A FEW DAYS.` → `FOR THE LOVE HE HAD TO HER.`

segments.voice: A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet. Ahavah, love. Four verses, four loves. First, love strong enough to bend time. That's Jacob. The Torah doesn't hide that this kind of love is real, and that it can change how a whole life feels. Second, love as a command. "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Those words follow straight after the Shema, and they raise a question teachers have asked: how can anyone be commanded to feel something? One answer the tradition gives: in the Torah, love is also something you do, with your heart, your soul and your might, which is to say with your whole life. Third, the neighbor. "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Tradition says Rabbi Akiva called this verse a great principle of the Torah. Fourth, later in the same chapter, the stranger. "Thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The same words, as thyself, now aimed at the outsider, with a reason: you know what it's like. So one root holds a young man's longing, a whole people's devotion, the person next door, and the immigrant down the road. Ahavah isn't kept for the ones who are easy to love. In every one of these verses, it's a word you can say and a thing you can do.
screen: `LOVE THAT BENDS TIME.` · `WITH ALL THINE HEART.` · `THE NEIGHBOR, AS THYSELF.` · `THE STRANGER, AS THYSELF.` · then, large: `AHAVAH.`

A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet: ahavah, love. For Rachel, for God, for the neighbor, and for the stranger. Today's word.
Your line: ahavah. In the Torah, love is felt, and it's also done. That's another day up the hill.

1370.title: L-M-D
1370.hook: lamad, limmud, talmid, Talmud: learning and teaching share a root
1370.howItsDone: Jews study Torah and Talmud in houses of study, synagogues and homes, often in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and arguing over each line together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-H-V: ahavah, love for Rachel, for God, for the neighbor and the stranger. Your line was ahavah. Today, a root you first met as an example.

In a beit midrash, a house of study, the room is loud. Two people sit across from each other over one open page. One reads a line aloud. The other says, no, that can't be what it means, and points at the next line. They push back and forth, sometimes for a long while on a few sentences. Who's the teacher here? Watch long enough and it's hard to say. Each one is learning, and each one is teaching, often in the same breath. Hebrew has a root that refuses to keep those two apart.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM, ONE OPEN PAGE.` → `TWO PEOPLE PUSHING BACK.` → `WHO'S THE TEACHER?`

segments.voice: L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet. You met these letters as the example when the roots began: talmid, melamed, Talmud. Today, what the root does. First, one verse, both ways. At Horeb, God tells Moses to gather the people "that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and that they may teach their children." Learn, and teach: the same three letters, a few words apart. Second, teach. Later Moses says: "And ye shall teach them your children." The same root, in a form that means making someone else learn. Not two words: one root, facing two ways. Third, the book. The collection of rabbinic study, argument and story is called the Talmud, from these same letters. Its name is study. Fourth, who learns from whom. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, records Rabbi Chanina saying he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and from his students most of all. And the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. So the teacher is always also a student, and the arrow points either way across the table. Even Isaiah uses the root in his picture of peace: "neither shall they learn war any more." What people learn, they can also unlearn.
screen: `LEARN AND TEACH, ONE VERSE.` · `TEACH THEM YOUR CHILDREN.` · `THE TALMUD: A BOOK NAMED STUDY.` · `MOST OF ALL FROM MY STUDENTS.` · then, large: `LEARNING AND TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Look back over these roots: shalom, wholeness; bracha, blessing that bends; emet, truth with its first letter; shema, hearing that heeds; teshuvah, turning. Pick the one that stuck and shape it into a single sentence you could say plainly over dinner, with no notes. If you pray, you can bring that sentence into your prayer as something learned.
L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet: to learn and to teach. The letters of talmid, student, and of the Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: learning and teaching. One root, facing both ways across the table. Go gently.

1371.title: Y-R-A
1371.hook: yirah means both fear and awe
1371.howItsDone: The days from Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur are called the Days of Awe, and Jewish prayer books carry blessings for moments of wonder, such as seeing lightning or a great sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, L-M-D: talmid and Talmud, one root for learning and teaching. Your line was learning and teaching. Today, a root that holds fear and awe at once.

Jacob is running from his brother. Night falls on the road, and he lies down with a stone under his head. He dreams of a ladder set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels going up and down on it. Then he wakes on the same hard ground and says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." And the very next words: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place!" Afraid. Dreadful. Two English words, and in the Hebrew, both come from today's three letters.
screen: `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A LADDER IN A DREAM.` → `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef. Yirah: fear, and awe. Four scenes. First, Jacob. He was afraid, vayira, and the place was dreadful, nora. He doesn't flee this place; he's shaken by it, and calls it "none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Second, wisdom. A psalm says: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Some readers hear yirah there less as terror and more as the right kind of smallness: knowing the world is bigger than you, and that you are not its center. Third, fear beside trust. At the sea, after the crossing, Exodus says: "and the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses." Believed is a form of A-M-N, the root of steadiness from earlier this block. Fear and faith stand side by side. Fourth, how awe begins. Maimonides, in his Mishneh Torah, writes that when a person looks closely at the great and wondrous works of creation, love rises first, a longing to know. Right after, the person draws back, aware of how small and brief they are. That's yirah: fear that stays to look. The days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur are called the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe, from the same root as Jacob's dreadful place.
screen: `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.` · `THE BEGINNING OF WISDOM.` · `FEARED, AND BELIEVED.` · `LOVE, THEN DRAWING BACK.` · then, large: `AWE.`

segments.voice: Choose something close by and look at it as if for the first time: your own hand, its lines and joints, the fact that it moves when you ask; or the sky through a window; or your breath, coming in without being called. Stay with it until it gets a little strange, a little large, and let yourself be small next to it. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place.
Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef: fear and awe in one root. Jacob's dreadful place, and the Days of Awe. Today's word.
Your line: awe. Yirah is the kind of fear that stays to look. Until tomorrow.

1372.title: Ch-Y-H
1372.hook: chai, chayim, life; chai adds to eighteen
1372.howItsDone: Jews raise a glass with l'chaim, to life, at celebrations, and some give gifts and donations in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition reads from the letters of chai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-R-A: yirah, fear and awe held in one word. Your line was awe. Today, a root you may already have raised a glass to.

A check for eighteen dollars. Not twenty, not fifteen. Eighteen. Or thirty-six, or a hundred and eighty. Open the cards at a bar mitzvah or a wedding and you may find these odd amounts, as if the guests shared a code. In a way they do. Hebrew letters double as numbers, and the word for alive, chai, is spelled with just two of them: chet and yud. By the old count tradition uses, chet is eight and yud is ten. Eighteen. So a gift of eighteen is a small wish folded into arithmetic, and the wish is life.
screen: `A CHECK FOR EIGHTEEN.` → `LETTERS ARE NUMBERS.` → `CHET AND YUD: CHAI.`

segments.voice: Ch-Y-H. Chet, yud, heh. Turn it four ways. First, the root itself. From these letters come chai, alive; chayah, a living creature; and the verb to live. Second, the word for life: chayim. It ends in the sound you hear on many Hebrew plurals, im. Some teachers like to read something into that, that a life is never just one thing. That's a reading, not a grammar rule, but it sticks. Third, a verse where the root goes to work. In Leviticus, God says of the laws, in the King James: "which if a man do, he shall live in them." The commandments are framed as something a person lives in, the way you live in a house. Fourth, what the rabbis did with that one word. In the Talmud, tractate Yoma, the sage Shmuel reads it closely: live by them, and not die by them. From this the rabbis teach that watching over a life, pikuach nefesh, pushes aside the rules of Shabbat. Someone collapses on a Saturday afternoon: you drive, you call, you do what saves them, and the law itself tells you to. So the root that rides on a toast and hides in the number eighteen is also a rule with real weight. The law is for living.
screen: `CH-Y-H: ALIVE, A CREATURE, TO LIVE.` · `CHAYIM: LIFE, WITH A PLURAL SOUND.` · `HE SHALL LIVE IN THEM.` · `LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.` · then, large: `חַיִּים`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person or place that keeps life going: a food bank, a clinic, a friend raising money, a neighbor who could use a meal. Picture a gift for them in eighteens, eighteen dollars or cents or minutes or words of thanks; the size isn't the point, the number carries the wish. Hold them in mind and say the word quietly, chai, and if you pray, you can ask a blessing on it.
Ch-Y-H. Chet, yud, heh: the root of chai, alive, and chayim, life. This week's roots ran stop, turn, pray, love, learn, awe, and now life. Today's word.
Your line: l'chaim, to life. The law, read this way, is for living. That's the week, with a glass raised.
